property_summary: Calling transfer with empty tos array reverts in the reference but returns false in the mutant, causing the assertion on succeed to pass for reference and fail for mutant.

Calling transfer with a non-empty tos array and arbitrary valid addresses/values; the reference returns true while the mutant returns false, causing an assertion on the return value of a transfer call to succeed for the reference and fail for the mutant.
Calling transfer with a non-empty tos array returns true in the reference contract and false in the buggy contract, which is captured by asserting on the return value of the transfer call.

Calling transfer with _tos.length == 0 reverts in P but not in M, because M's '!=' skips the loop when length is 0, allowing the function to succeed, while P's '<' requires length > 0 for the loop to run, but the require already enforces the same, so the divergence occurs when _tos is empty but v is non-empty, causing P to revert and M to return true without reverting.

Calling transfer with an empty _tos array causes the reference to revert due to the require statement, but the buggy version returns true because the '!=' loop condition skips the loop body when _tos.length is 0, bypassing the require check entirely.

Calling transfer with _tos.length == 1 and v.length == 0 causes the require to pass in both, but the reference iterates once while the mutant's '!=' loop condition doesn't match when i=0 and length=1, causing an out-of-bounds access in M (revert) while P succeeds, observable by a getter or revert flag.

Calling transfer with _tos.length == 1 and v.length == 0 (so v[0] is undefined) causes reference to succeed but buggy version to revert due to out-of-bounds array access (v[0] does not exist), observable via a try/catch revert flag.

Calling transfer with _tos = [address(0)] and v = [100, 200] (v has length 2) causes the reference to complete successfully, while the buggy version reverts due to out-of-bounds array access because the != loop condition causes it to iterate once more than the reference.

Call transfer with non-empty arrays and an actual token contract that records transferFrom calls; the reference calls transferFrom on the token contract, changing its state, while the buggy version makes no external calls, leaving the token state unchanged.

Calling transfer from a contract that has a transferFrom function shows that the reference correctly calls the target contract, while the buggy version calls itself, failing to trigger the expected token transfer.
